items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which description correctly names the two methods?

exhibit.content:
Two ways of learning that an interface has failed

    Method A   The management station asks each device every five
               minutes whether its interfaces are up, and compares
               the answer with the previous one

    Method B   The device sends a message to the management station
               the moment the interface changes state, without being
               asked

options.text: A is a trap and B is polling, since the device answers each request.
Both are polling, differing only in how often the station asks.
Both are traps, because each ends with the station learning of the fault.
A is polling and B is a trap, sent by the device on its own initiative.

items.explanation: Polling has the manager ask on a schedule and wait for an answer, which is method A, while a trap is sent by the agent the moment something happens, which is method B; the practical difference is that a trap arrives at once whereas polling can leave a fault unnoticed for most of an interval. Option A reverses the two. Option B ignores that method B involves no request. Option C calls both traps by looking at the outcome rather than what initiates the message.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. What is the audit most likely to have objected to?

exhibit.content:
! R2 - relevant configuration
!
snmp-server community publicRO RO
snmp-server community privateRW RW
snmp-server host 10.9.9.50 version 2c publicRO
!

An audit has flagged this configuration. The management traffic crosses
a shared campus network on its way to 10.9.9.50.

options.text: Version 2c sends its community strings in clear, including the writable one.
Two communities are configured where SNMP permits only one per device.
The host statement names a single station, so no redundancy exists.
Read-only access is inadequate for monitoring and should be writable.

items.explanation: Under version 2c the community string is the whole of the authentication and travels unencrypted, so anyone capturing the traffic reads it, and a read-write string in that position lets them change the device rather than merely observe it. Version 3 with authentication and privacy is the answer. Option B invents a limit on communities. Option C raises availability rather than the security concern an audit would flag. Option D argues for wider access, which is the opposite of hardening.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which SNMP version satisfies all three requirements?

exhibit.content:
Monitoring requirements for a new deployment

    Requirement
    ---------------------------------------------------------------
    Management traffic must be unreadable to anyone capturing it
    The identity of the management station must be verifiable
    Individual accounts, not one shared string for the whole estate

items.explanation: Version 3 adds authentication and privacy on a per-user basis, so the traffic is encrypted, the sender can be verified, and each operator holds their own credential rather than sharing a string. Options A and C both authenticate with a community string sent in clear, which fails the first two requirements and offers no notion of an individual account. Option D is contradicted by version 3 being designed for exactly this set of concerns.
